claim: The pupil is primarily regulated by prevailing light levels but is also modulated by perceptual and attentional factors.
source: The pupil is primarily regulated by prevailing light levels but is also modulated by perceptual and attentional factors.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about pupillary control mechanisms.

claim: In some participants viewing a bistable-rotating cylinder, pupil diameter oscillated in phase with the ambiguous perception, more dilated when the black surface was in front.
source: In some participants, pupil diameter oscillated in phase with the ambiguous perception, more dilated when the black surface was in front.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of pupil size during the bistable perception task, as shown in the results.

claim: The magnitude of pupil oscillation predicts autistic traits of participants, assessed by the Autism-Spectrum Quotient AQ.
source: Importantly, the magnitude of oscillation predicts autistic traits of participants, assessed by the Autism-Spectrum Quotient AQ.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between pupil modulation and AQ scores presented in the results.

claim: High AQ participants focus on the front surface of the rotating cylinder.
source: high AQ participants focus on the front surface of the rotating cylinder
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of pupil responses and their correlation with AQ scores.

claim: Low AQ participants distribute attention to both surfaces in a more global, holistic style.
source: those with low AQ distribute attention to both surfaces in a more global, holistic style
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of pupil responses and their correlation with AQ scores.

claim: This is the first evidence that pupillometry reliably tracks inter-individual differences in perceptual styles.
source: This is the first evidence that pupillometry reliably tracks inter-individual differences in perceptual styles
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings, based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Pupillometry tracks perceptual styles quickly and objectively, without interfering with spontaneous perceptual strategies.
source: it does so quickly and objectively, without interfering with spontaneous perceptual strategies
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental design and results showing correlations in free-viewing conditions.

claim: The ability to form a whole from parts is a major developmental step in childhood and a component of how we define intelligence.
source: The ability to form a whole from parts, ignoring details to form meaningful classes, is a major developmental step in childhood and a component of how we define intelligence – one of the tests for IQ in the standard Wechsler Scale.
evidence: This draws from established knowledge about cognitive development and intelligence testing.

claim: Autistic observers show slower responses to global structure.
source: autistic observers show slower responses to global structure (Van der Hallen et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Van der Hallen et al., 2015.

claim: Autistic observers show enhanced processing of local features.
source: enhanced processing of local features (Mottron et al., 2006; Muth et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mottron et al., 2006 and Muth et al., 2014.

claim: There is increasing interest in determining whether differences in the preference for local or global styles are also associated with autistic traits in the typical population.
source: There is increasing interest in determining whether differences in the preference for local or global styles are also associated with autistic traits in the typical population, supporting the dimensional view of autistic disorders, where people with and without ASD diagnosis lay along a continuum and differ only quantitatively, not qualitatively (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001; Constantino and Todd, 2003; Ruzich et al., 2015; Skuse et al., 2009; Wheelwright et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the dimensional view of autism.

claim: Not all attempts have been successful at showing a local-global difference in neurotypical individuals.
source: However, not all attempts have been successful at showing a local-global difference in neurotypical individuals (Cribb et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cribb et al., 2016.

claim: The limited reliability and validity of tests for local-global preference may result from the fact that they correlate little with each other and probably measure very different combinations of abilities and constructs.
source: which may a result from the limited reliability and validity of the tests, which correlate little with each other and probably measure very different combinations of abilities and constructs (Milne and Szczerbinski, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Milne and Szczerbinski, 2009.

claim: 50 randomly selected neuro-typical adults with variable degrees of autistic traits were tested.
source: We tested 50 randomly selected neuro-typical adults with variable degrees of autistic traits, as measured by the Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ)
evidence: This describes the participant sample in the study.

claim: The Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ) is a tool developed to characterize the normal spectrum of subclinical autistic behaviours in the general population.
source: as measured by the Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ), a tool developed to characterize the normal spectrum of subclinical autistic behaviours in the general population (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baron-Cohen et al., 2001.

claim: Pupil-size is modulated by cognitive and top-down factors, such as perceived rather than physical luminance.
source: which is has shown to be modulated by cognitive and top-down factors, such as perceived rather than physical luminance, and shifts in attention from dark to bright surfaces (Binda and Murray, 2015; Binda et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Binda and Murray, 2015 and Binda et al., 2014.

claim: Attending to a bright or dark surface is sufficient to evoke pupil constrictions or dilations respectively, tracking the focus of 'feature-based' attention.
source: Specifically, attending to a bright or dark surface is sufficient to evoke pupil constrictions or dilations respectively, tracking the focus of 'feature-based' attention (Binda et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Binda et al., 2014.

claim: On average, perceived direction alternated every 5.5 s (0.21 ± 0.01 perceptual switches per second).
source: On average, perceived direction alternated every 5.5 s (0.21 ± 0.01 perceptual switches per second)
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The between-subject variability of switch rate did not correlate with autistic traits (Pearson's r = 0.02 [-0.26 0.29], p=0.901, Bayes Factor [BF]=0.1).
source: the between-subject variability of switch rate did not correlate with autistic traits (Pearson's r = 0.02 [-0.26 0.29], p=0.901, Bayes Factor [BF]=0.1)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The pupil dilated transiently at or just after each perceptual switch, irrespective of whether perception switches toward a black or a white foreground.
source: First, as reported previously for binocular rivalry (Einhäuser et al., 2008), the pupil dilated transiently at or just after each perceptual switch; this effect is seen on both blue and red traces, meaning that the dilation occurs irrespective of whether perception switches toward a black or a white foreground.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B and cited work on binocular rivalry.

claim: The pupil was more dilated when the foreground was black and more constricted when it was white.
source: However, there is also a second kind of pupil modulation that depends on the direction of the shift: the pupil was more dilated when the foreground was black and more constricted when it was white.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pupillary modulation occurs during binocular rivalry between stimuli of different luminances, leading to pupillary constriction when the brighter stimulus dominates.
source: This is similar to the pupillary modulation that occurs during binocular rivalry between stimuli of different luminances, leading to pupillary constriction when the brighter stimulus dominates (Naber et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Naber et al., 2011.

claim: The luminance-dependent pupil modulation is a purely perceptual effect, as the stimulus luminance is constant throughout the experiment.
source: This luminance-dependent modulation is a purely perceptual effect, as the stimulus luminance is constant throughout the experiment.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental design where physical luminance does not change.

claim: The constriction when the foreground was white probably results from participants attending more to the foreground than the background.
source: The constriction when the foreground was white probably results from participants attending more to the foreground than the background, as it is known that attending to white constricts the pupil (Binda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citation to Binda et al., 2013.

claim: If participants were to distribute attention evenly between the back and the front surfaces (or rapidly switch attention between them), no pupil difference would be expected.
source: On the other hand, if participants were to distribute attention evenly between the back and the front surfaces (or rapidly switch attention between them), no pupil difference would be expected.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the known effects of attention on pupil size.

claim: Local and global perceptual styles are associated with high and low autistic traits.
source: As these two strategies correspond well to the local and global perceptual styles associated with high and low autistic traits (Happé and Frith, 2006; Grinter et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Happé and Frith, 2006 and Grinter et al., 2009.

claim: Pupil modulation should be more prominent in participants with higher AQ scores.
source: pupil modulation should be more prominent in participants with higher AQ scores
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the relationship between perceptual styles and autistic traits.

claim: There was considerable variation in luminance-dependent pupil change among the sample of typical young adults.
source: Figure 1D shows that, in our sample of typical young adults, there was considerable variation in luminance-dependent pupil change pupil modulation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The signed amplitude of the modulation was significantly positive in 20 out of the 50 participants.
source: The signed amplitude of the modulation was significantly positive in 20 out of the 50 participants.
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the experimental data.

claim: The amplitude of modulation was highly correlated with AQ scores (r = 0.70,[0.52:0.82] p<10−5, BF >105).
source: Crucially, the amplitude of modulation, which we suggest is an index of perceptual style, was highly correlated with AQ scores (r = 0.70,[0.52:0.82] p<10−5, BF >105).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: AQ scores did not correlate with the general dilation that followed all perceptual switches (r = 0.06,[-0.22:0.33], p=0.678, BF = 0.1).
source: Importantly, the correlation was specific to this particular pupillometric index: AQ scores did not correlate with the general dilation that followed all perceptual switches (r = 0.06,[-0.22:0.33], p=0.678, BF = 0.1: Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Most subjects reported that they found the instructions to attend globally or locally difficult to follow, and that they tended to lapse into their more natural viewing style.
source: Most subjects reported that they found the instructions difficult to follow, and that they tended to lapse into their more natural viewing style.
evidence: This is based on subjective reports from participants.

claim: The instructions significantly affected the luminance-dependent pupil modulation (0.005 ± 0.007 mm when instruction favoured the global strategy; 0.029 ± 0.008 mm when they favoured the local strategy).
source: Nevertheless, the instructions significantly affected the luminance-dependent pupil modulation (0.005 ± 0.007 mm when instruction favoured the global strategy; 0.029 ± 0.008 mm when they favoured the local strategy), which was greater when the local strategy was encouraged (paired t-test: t:(9) = −2.72, p=0.024).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The pupil can be a more sensitive (as well as more objective) probe of perceptual style than are subjective reports.
source: This supports the suggestion that pupil modulation is driven by perceptual style, and further also shows that the pupil can be a more sensitive (as well as more objective) probe of perceptual style than are subjective reports.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that pupil measures showed effects even when subjective reports indicated difficulty following instructions.

claim: Participants reported the number of speed changes in the dots of the cued surface with an average of 62 ± 2% correct responses.
source: To monitor compliance, participants reported the number of speed changes in the dots of the cued surface (ignoring changes in the other surface), which they did with an average of 62 ± 2% correct responses (uncorrelated with AQ, r = 0.24 [-0.04 0.49], p=0.090, BF = 0.5).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data.

claim: There was a strong modulation of pupil size in the averaged data, depending on whether the white or the dark surface was attended in the feature-based attention experiment.
source: Under these conditions, there was a strong modulation of pupil size in the averaged data, depending on whether the white or the dark surface was attended (Figure 2B), consistent with the reported effects of feature-based attention on pupil size (Binda et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and consistent with cited work.

claim: In the feature-based attention experiment where viewing style was constrained by the task, all subjects tended to show front-color dependent pupil modulation, and it was not correlated with AQ (r = 0.20 [-0.08:0.46], p=0.156, BF = 0.3).
source: However, in this experiment, where viewing style was constrained by the task, all subjects tended to show front-color dependent pupil modulation, and it was not correlated with AQ (r = 0.20 [-0.08:0.46], p=0.156, BF = 0.3, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The correlation between AQ and pupil difference was strong and significant in both groups of 25 participants (first subset: r = 0.75, p<10−4, BF >103; second subset: r = 0.64, p<0.001, BF = 54.3).
source: The correlation between AQ and pupil difference was strong and significant in both groups (Figure 3A, first subset: r = 0.75, p<10−4, BF >103; Figure 3B, second subset: r = 0.64, p<0.001, BF = 54.3).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: The effect was replicated in a slightly different condition tested in 26 participants (swapping the motion directions of white and black dots, r = 0.66 p<0.001, BF = 85.3).
source: We further replicated the effect in a slightly different condition, tested in 26 participants (swapping the motion directions of white and black dots, Figure 3C, r = 0.66 p<0.001, BF = 85.3)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The three correlation coefficients are statistically indistinguishable (Fisher's Z test; all p-values>0.23), implying that the results are robust.
source: the three correlation coefficients are statistically indistinguishable (Fisher's Z test; all p-values>0.23), implying that the results are robust.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing the three replications.

claim: All but one correlation coefficients between pupil difference and AQ subscales were positive and significant.
source: All but one correlation coefficients were positive and significant (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The strongest correlations were with the Communication and Social Skills subscales, and weakest with 'Attention to Detail' scores.
source: The strongest correlations were with the Communication and Social Skills subscales, and weakest with 'Attention to Detail' scores (discussed later).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Speed-change detection performance was generally better when targets occurred on the front than on the rear surface (paired t-test on d-prime values: t(24)=4.43, p<0.001).
source: Speed-change detection performance was generally better when targets occurred on the front than on the rear surface (Figure 4C paired t-test on d-prime values: t(24)=4.43, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In the double-task experiment, AQ correlated neither with the difference in performance (r = −0.03 [-0.42 0.37], p=0.869, BF = 0.2) nor with the pupil difference (r = −0.27 [-0.60 0.14], p=0.187, BF = 0.4).
source: However, AQ correlated neither with the difference in performance (Figure 4D, r = −0.03 [-0.42 0.37], p=0.869, BF = 0.2) nor with the pupil difference (Figure 4B r = −0.27 [-0.60 0.14], p=0.187, BF = 0.4).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figures 4B and 4D.

claim: The double-task setting (necessary to obtain a psychophysical index of attention distribution) interfered with participants' natural viewing style, biasing all towards a 'local' processing style.
source: This shows that the double-task setting (necessary to obtain a psychophysical index of attention distribution) interfered with participants' natural viewing style, biasing all towards a 'local' processing style, focusing on one surface at a time to detect the speed changes.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation with AQ in the double-task condition.

claim: The double-task setting undermined the possibility of estimating the inter-individual differences that spontaneously emerge in the free-viewing conditions of the main experiment.
source: This clearly undermined the possibility of estimating the inter-individual differences that spontaneously emerge in the free-viewing conditions of the main experiment.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between the main experiment and the double-task experiment results.

claim: Some participants spontaneously reported that they attended locally to only the front surface, while others reported that they had to attend globally to the whole configuration.
source: Some participants spontaneously reported their perceptual experience: of these some reported that they attending locally to only the front surface, while others reported that they had to attend globally to the whole configuration, both front and rear, in order to perceive the rotation.
evidence: This is based on spontaneous subjective reports from participants.

claim: The spontaneous reports from participants with high and low AQ provide qualitative support for the interpretation that high AQ participants focus locally and low AQ participants attend globally.
source: These spontaneous reports (respectively from participants with high and low AQ) provide qualitative support for our interpretation.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of spontaneous reports and their relationship to AQ scores.

claim: The underlying mechanisms of preference for local versus global are essentially unknown.
source: Although preference for local versus global has been extensively investigated and has come to be a defining feature of Autistic Spectrum Disorders (Van der Hallen et al., 2015; Muth et al., 2014), its underlying mechanisms are essentially unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Local-global preference could be a perceptual style, depending on differences in the bottom-up transmission of sensory information.
source: It could be a perceptual style, depending on differences in the bottom-up transmission of sensory information (Mottron et al., 2006; Mottron et al., 2003; Plaisted et al., 2003)
evidence: This is a speculative possibility supported by citations.

claim: Local-global preference could have a cognitive or attentional basis, depending on a preference to maintain a narrow focus of attention.
source: but it could also have a cognitive or attentional basis, depending on a preference to maintain a narrow focus of attention (Happé and Frith, 2006; Plaisted et al., 1999)
evidence: This is a speculative possibility supported by citations.

claim: Local-global preference could result from a relative inability to divide or switch attention between multiple targets.
source: or a relative inability to divide or switch attention between multiple targets (Behrmann et al., 2006; Frith and Happé, 1994; Happé and Frith, 1996; Happé and Booth, 2008)
evidence: This is a speculative possibility supported by citations.

claim: The results clearly show that autistic traits are associated with a more local perceptual style.
source: While our results do not distinguish between the different possible explanations of perceptual styles, they clearly show that autistic traits are associated with a more local perceptual style.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between pupil modulation and AQ scores.

claim: There is an ongoing dispute about whether autistic traits are distributed continuously amongst the population with ASD diagnosis at an extreme, or whether the distinction is more categorical.
source: There is an ongoing dispute about whether autistic traits are distributed continuously amongst the population with ASD diagnosis at an extreme, or whether the distinction is more categorical (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001; Constantino and Todd, 2003; Ruzich et al., 2015; Skuse et al., 2009; Wheelwright et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of debate in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The hypothesis of a 'Broader Autistic Phenotype' strongly predicts that local-global preference should be continuously distributed and correlated with autistic traits in the neurotypical population.
source: The hypothesis of a 'Broader Autistic Phenotype' strongly predicts that local-global preference should be continuously distributed and correlated with autistic traits in the neurotypical population (Cribb et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by citation.

claim: Many of the classic tests show very low or insignificant correlations with autistic traits.
source: However, many of the classic tests show very low or insignificant correlations with autistic traits (Cribb et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cribb et al., 2016.

claim: The pupillometry index shows the strongest correlation with autistic traits reported so far in a large group of participants, explaining about 50% of the variance in AQ scores.
source: Our experiment describes a pupillometry index with the strongest correlation with autistic traits reported so far in a large group of participants, explaining about 50% of the variance in AQ scores.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation coefficient (r=0.70) which explains approximately 50% of variance.

claim: The test-retest reliability of the autistic questionnaire has been reported to be around 0.75.
source: The test-retest reliability of the autistic questionnaire has been reported to be around 0.75 (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001; Hoekstra et al., 2008; Kurita et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baron-Cohen et al., 2001, Hoekstra et al., 2008, and Kurita et al., 2005.

claim: In the 22 participants who performed both the main experiment and the swapped-direction, the correlation of pupil modulation in the two tasks was 0.68 ([0.36:0.86], p<0.001, BF = 62.7).
source: In the 22 participants who performed both the main experiment and the swapped-direction, the correlation of pupil modulation in the two tasks was 0.68 ([0.36:0.86], p<0.001, BF = 62.7).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The 'Attention to Detail' subscale seems to have the lowest construct validity of the five subscales.
source: However, the 'Attention to Detail' subscale seems to have the lowest construct validity of the five subscales
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence cited below.

claim: The 'Attention to Detail' subscale had the lowest performance in classifying individuals with and without ASD diagnosis in a sample of 350 adults, with 130 ASD diagnoses.
source: it had the lowest performance in classifying individuals with and without ASD diagnosis in a sample of 350 adults, with 130 ASD diagnoses (Lundqvist and Lindner, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lundqvist and Lindner, 2017.

claim: The 'Attention to Detail' subscale had the lowest correlation with the general AQ score in a sample of 2343 typical individuals.
source: it had the lowest correlation with the general AQ score in a sample of 2343 typical individuals (Palmer et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Palmer et al., 2015.

claim: In the current sample, scores on the 'Attention to Detail' subscale did not correlate significantly with the overall AQ score.
source: and, in our sample, scores on the 'Attention to Detail' subscale did not correlate significantly with the overall AQ score.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Among the items contributing to the 'Attention to Detail' subscale, only four actually relate to perceptual phenomena, the others being focused on memory and cognition.
source: It is also worth noting that among the items contributing to the 'Attention to Detail' subscale, only four actually relate to perceptual phenomena (e.g. 'I usually concentrate more on the whole picture, rather than the small details."), the others being focused on memory and cognition (e.g. 'I am fascinated by numbers.").
evidence: This is based on examination of the questionnaire items.

claim: There is a general difficulty in measuring local-global preference, either with self-report or with laboratory tests.
source: All this highlights a general difficulty in measuring local-global preference, either with self-report or with laboratory tests.
evidence: This is inferred from the discussion of the limitations of existing measures.

claim: By combining the objectivity of pupillometry and the flexibility of a perceptual task involving bistable perception, a very reliable and precise measure of inter-individual differences can be achieved.
source: However, by combining the objectivity of pupillometry and the flexibility of a perceptual task involving bistable perception, we can achieve a very reliable and precise measure of inter-individual differences.
evidence: This is inferred from the strong correlations obtained in the study.

claim: There is growing interest in relating differences among individuals in their performance in perceptual tasks, with states or traits of their personality.
source: There is growing interest in relating differences among individuals in their performance in perceptual tasks, with states or traits of their personality (Tadin, 2015; Eldar et al., 2013; Antinori et al., 2016; Wilson et al., 2016; Maclean and Arnell, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing this research trend.

claim: The amount of explained variance in relating perceptual performance to personality is usually lower than in the current experiment.
source: However, the amount of explained variance is usually lower than in our experiment
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with the cited literature.

claim: The current study is a rare case where a physiological measure obtained from a laboratory experiment explains a large portion of inter-individual differences in the way we feel and behave.
source: which is a rare case where a physiological measure obtained from a laboratory experiment explains a large portion of inter-individual differences in the way we feel and behave.
evidence: This is inferred from the high correlation obtained and comparison with the literature.

claim: Free-viewing of the bistable stimulus was essential to obtain the clear correlation with AQ.
source: To obtain the clear correlation with AQ, free-viewing of the bistable stimulus was essential
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between free-viewing and constrained viewing conditions.

claim: The correlation between pupillometry and AQ scores was eliminated when cueing attention, either explicitly or implicitly.
source: the correlation between pupillometry and AQ scores was eliminated when cueing attention, either explicitly, by instructing participants to attend globally/locally or by indicating that the surface formed by white or black dots alone is task-relevant, or implicitly, by introducing a task that is best performed by attending a single surface at a time.
evidence: This is supported by the results from the feature-based attention and double-task experiments.

claim: Previous work has shown differences in bistable viewing that are related to autism.
source: Although previous work has shown differences in bistable viewing that are related to autism [(Robertson et al., 2013); but see also (Said et al., 2013)]
evidence: This is supported by citations to Robertson et al., 2013 and Said et al., 2013.

claim: The dynamics of perceptual oscillations between the two directions of motion were uncorrelated with autistic traits.
source: we found that the dynamics of perceptual oscillations between the two directions of motion were uncorrelated with autistic traits.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis showing no correlation between switch rate and AQ.

claim: The correlation with AQ was only revealed when taking pupillometry measures to index how attention was distributed during the bistable perception.
source: The correlation with AQ was only revealed only when taking pupillometry measures to index how attention was distributed during the bistable perception.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of results across different measures.

claim: The current study strengthens previous claims that pupil size is modulated not only by light, but also by perceptual 'top-down' processes.
source: The current study strengthens previous claims that pupil size is modulated not only by light, but also by perceptual 'top-down' processes (Binda and Murray, 2015; Mathôt and Van der Stigchel, 2015; Laeng and Endestad, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the current findings and citations to previous work.

claim: The neural substrates of pupillary modulatory mechanisms are beginning to be unveiled, involving pre-frontal input into the circuit of the pupillary response to light.
source: The neural substrates of these modulatory mechanisms are beginning to be unveiled, involving pre-frontal input into the circuit of the pupillary response to light (Ebitz and Moore, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ebitz and Moore, 2017.

claim: The neural circuit of pupillary response may include the visual cortex.
source: which in turn may include the visual cortex (Binda and Gamlin, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Binda and Gamlin, 2017.

claim: Under appropriate conditions (free viewing a bistable stimulus with brighter and darker components), pupil size can provide an objective physiological correlate of conscious perception.
source: As we show here, under appropriate conditions (free viewing a bistable stimulus with brighter and darker components), this variable can provide an objective physiological correlate of conscious perception, so reliable that it can successfully reveal subtle inter-individual differences that are hard to study psychophysically.
evidence: This is inferred from the strong correlations obtained in the study.

claim: The pupillometry method is quick, easy, and objective, and requires only relatively simple, portable apparatus.
source: The method is quick, easy, and objective, and requires only relatively simple, portable apparatus.
evidence: This is based on the practical characteristics of the experimental method used.

claim: The pupillometry method can form the basis for tests suitable for clinical populations, possibly providing a new powerful tool for identifying anomalies in perception that are predictive of ASD.
source: We hope it can form the basis for tests suitable for clinical populations, possibly providing a new powerful tool for identifying anomalies in perception that are predictive of ASD.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications.

claim: A total of 62 subjects (42 women; age (mean ± SD): 25.53 ± 4.04) were recruited in three groups.
source: We recruited a total of 62 subjects (42 women; age (mean ± SD): 25.53 ± 4.04), in three groups (25 in the first, 26 in the second and 11 in the last).
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: All participants were students from the University of Pisa or Florence, in at least their third year.
source: All were students from the University of Pisa or Florence, in at least their third year.
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: All participants reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and had no diagnosed neurological condition.
source: All reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and had no diagnosed neurological condition.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for participants.

claim: The number of participants recruited for the study was selected to provide a large effect size as indicated by a priori power analysis (effect size: 0.50, α = 0.05, two-tail) that reveals that in order to reach a power (1−β) of 0.8 a sample size of 26 subjects was needed.
source: The number of participants recruited for the study was selected to provide a large effect size as indicated by a priori power analysis (effect size: 0.50, α = 0.05, two-tail) that reveals that in order to reach a power (1−β) of 0.8 a sample size of 26 subjects was needed.
evidence: This describes the rationale for sample size selection.

claim: All tested subjects scored below 32 on the AQ, which is the threshold above which a clinical assessment is recommended.
source: All tested subjects scored below 32, which is the threshold above which a clinical assessment is recommended (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001).
evidence: This describes the AQ scores of the sample and cites the clinical threshold.

claim: The mean (SD) of the AQ scores was 14.85 (6.73).
source: The mean (SD) of the scores was 14.85 (6.73)
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic of the sample.

claim: AQ scores were normally distributed (JB = 1.42 p=0.37).
source: scores were normally distributed (see Figure 3D), as measured by the Jarque-Bera goodness-of-fit test of composite normality (JB = 1.42 p=0.37).
evidence: This is supported by statistical test and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The stimulus comprised 150 leftward-moving white dots and 150 rightward-moving black dots, giving the immediate impression of a cylinder rotating in depth at 10 revolutions per minute.
source: We tracked pupil-size while participants viewed an ambiguous dynamic stimulus comprising 150 leftward-moving white dots and 150 rightward-moving black dots, giving the immediate impression of a cylinder rotating in depth at 10 revolutions per minute (see Figure 1A and Video 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental stimulus, shown in Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: The depth of the dots was ambiguous, so either dot-group could be seen in front, resulting in either clockwise or counter-clockwise rotation.
source: As the depth of the dots was ambiguous, either dot-group (tagged by luminance and direction) could be seen in front, resulting in either clockwise or counter-clockwise rotation.
